book-110-1.questionInPlainEnglish: What antibody part does the source illustration circle?
book-110-1.explanation: The source marks an antigen-binding arm, called Fab. It contains parts of one heavy and one light chain; their variable regions form the surface that recognizes a target.
optionExplanations: Fab is the antigen-binding fragment and matches the source's indicated arm.
Fc is the constant stem, not the target-binding arm.
A heavy chain extends through both arm and stem and is not the name of the whole circled fragment.
The hinge is the flexible joint where arms meet the stem.

quickCheck.question: Which antibody fragment directly binds an epitope?

book-110-1.sourceNote: Illustration-dependent: Color Plate 21 identifies Fab. The textual key and rationale agree; the arm cannot be located from the stem without the plate.

book-110-11.questionInPlainEnglish: Whose antibodies make up most serum antibody in a full-term newborn?
book-110-11.explanation: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta, especially late in pregnancy. It supplies temporary protection while the infant's own antibody production develops.
optionExplanations: Infant IgA is not the predominant serum antibody at birth.
The infant makes relatively little IgG before birth.
Infant IgM can be made, but normally is not the dominant neonatal serum antibody.
Maternal IgG is actively transferred across the placenta and predominates.
book-110-11.memory: A full-term newborn borrows mother's IgG.

quickCheck.question: Which antibody class crosses the placenta efficiently?

book-110-30.questionInPlainEnglish: What immunoglobulin pattern is expected in Bruton disease?
book-110-30.explanation: Bruton disease blocks normal B-cell maturation. With very few functioning mature B cells, all antibody classes are profoundly reduced; small residual amounts, especially IgG, can remain.
optionExplanations: Elevated IgE contradicts the broad failure of antibody production.
Elevated IgG contradicts the expected low antibody levels.
Isolated low IgA describes a different deficiency pattern.
Absence of all immunoglobulins is the book's simplified description of profound panhypogammaglobulinemia.
book-110-30.memory: Bruton blocks B-cell maturation and broadly lowers antibodies.

quickCheck.question: Are T-cell numbers usually preserved in Bruton disease?

book-110-30.sourceNote: All immunoglobulins absent is a simplified exam description. Bruton agammaglobulinemia usually produces profoundly reduced levels, and some residual immunoglobulin may be measurable.

book-110-56.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement about antibody light chains is true?
book-110-56.explanation: Light chains come in two types, kappa and lambda. Each antibody monomer carries two light chains of the same type, and both help build its antigen-binding arms.
optionExplanations: A monomer has two light chains, not one.
Kappa and lambda are the two light-chain types.
Each light chain has variable and constant regions, not only constant regions.
Light chains belong to Fab; Fc is formed from heavy-chain portions.
book-110-56.memory: Two light chains, one type per antibody.

quickCheck.question: Can one ordinary antibody monomer have one kappa and one lambda light chain?
quickCheck.answer: No; its two light chains are the same type.

book-110-58.questionInPlainEnglish: Which cells are used in the classic production of monoclonal antibody reagents?
book-110-58.explanation: A hybridoma combines an antibody-making B/plasma cell with a continuously growing myeloma cell. This lets one selected clone produce the same antibody repeatedly.
optionExplanations: T cells do not normally secrete immunoglobulin.
Human plasma cells make antibodies, but this alone does not describe the classic immortal reagent-producing cell line.
Mouse plasma cells can supply specificity, but alone do not grow indefinitely.
Hybridomas unite specific antibody production with sustained cell growth.
book-110-58.memory: Hybridoma combines an antibody factory with a lasting growth engine.

quickCheck.question: What two capabilities are combined in a hybridoma?
quickCheck.answer: Specific antibody secretion and continuous growth.

book-110-58.sourceNote: The stem is imprecise: a single normal plasma-cell clone also produces monoclonal antibody. Hybridoma is the intended classic laboratory-production answer; modern recombinant methods also exist.

book-110-70.explanation: Many contact allergens are small haptens. After binding skin proteins, they create targets recognized by sensitized T cells, causing a delayed rash.
optionExplanations: Preformed IgE causes immediate allergy, not classic delayed contact dermatitis.
Neutrophil influx is not its defining antigen-specific mechanism.
The primary reaction occurs at skin contact sites rather than chiefly in airways.
A hapten binding a carrier protein is the common initiating pattern.
book-110-70.memory: A small contact chemical becomes visible to immunity when attached to protein.

quickCheck.question: Which cells drive classic allergic contact dermatitis?

book-110-71.questionInPlainEnglish: What does a raised CRP generally indicate?
book-110-71.explanation: CRP is an acute-phase protein made mainly by the liver during inflammation. It indicates an inflammatory response but does not identify the cause by itself.
optionExplanations: CRP is not a direct measurement of neutrophil swallowing ability.
Ongoing inflammation is the correct general interpretation.
Many conditions raise CRP, so it is not diagnostic of rheumatic fever.
CRP can rise in inflammatory cardiovascular conditions; a universal decrease is incorrect.
book-110-71.memory: CRP is an inflammation alarm, not a disease name tag.

quickCheck.question: Does high CRP identify one specific disease?

book-110-78.questionInPlainEnglish: What does a positive HBsAg usually indicate?
book-110-78.explanation: HBsAg is hepatitis B surface antigen. Its presence generally means current HBV infection, either acute or chronic; other markers and duration establish the stage.
optionExplanations: Resolved past infection usually has no detectable HBsAg and often has anti-HBs.
Current acute or chronic HBV infection is the intended interpretation.
Vaccination aims to produce anti-HBs antibody, not ongoing antigenemia.
A person with current HBsAg may be infectious, so this claim is incorrect.
book-110-78.memory: Antigen means viral material; anti-HBs means an antibody response.

quickCheck.question: Does HBsAg positivity alone prove chronic HBV?

book-110-78.sourceNote: HBsAg generally indicates current HBV infection, but transient antigen detection can occasionally follow recent vaccination. The source's absolute denial of any post-vaccine HBsAg is too strong. HBsAg alone does not quantify replication.

book-110-80.explanation: The heavy-chain constant region determines the class or isotype, such as IgG or IgM. Variable-region differences determine binding specificity rather than class.
optionExplanations: Heavy-chain type defines immunoglobulin class and is correct.
Inherited allelic differences within a class are allotypes.
One person can make several isotypes, so isotype is not constant across all their antibodies.
Variable-region antigenic features concern idiotype rather than isotype.

quickCheck.question: Which heavy chain identifies IgG?

book-135-1.questionInPlainEnglish: Which finding excludes this donor under the book's screening rules?
book-135-1.explanation: Donation removes red cells and reduces oxygen-carrying capacity. Her hematocrit of 35% is below the book's minimum, while her stated weight, pulse, and pressure meet its listed expectations.
optionExplanations: A pulse of 73 beats per minute is not too high.
110 pounds meets the conventional minimum weight used in this example.
A 35% hematocrit is below the source's stated minimum of 38%.
125/75 mm Hg is not a low blood pressure in this example.
book-135-1.memory: Donor red-cell screening protects the donor's oxygen supply.

quickCheck.question: What does hematocrit measure?
quickCheck.answer: The fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells.

book-135-1.sourceNote: Historical screening criteria are preserved for this exercise. Current donor hemoglobin/hematocrit requirements can depend on sex, donation type, jurisdiction, and permitted exceptions; 38% is not a universal present-day minimum.

book-135-2.questionInPlainEnglish: What volume results from the book's 10.5 mL/kg rule for a 95-pound donor?
book-135-2.explanation: Convert pounds to kilograms: 95/2.2 = 43.2 kg. Multiplying by 10.5 gives approximately 454 mL, including samples. This is the textbook calculation, not automatic donor eligibility.
optionExplanations: 367 mL does not result from the given weight-based formula.
378 mL is below the calculated 454 mL.
454 mL correctly rounds 43.2 × 10.5.
473 mL exceeds the amount calculated from the stated rule.
book-135-2.memory: Convert weight first, then multiply by the allowed volume per kilogram.

quickCheck.question: About how many kilograms is 95 pounds?

book-135-2.sourceNote: This is only the textbook's 10.5 mL/kg calculation. A 95-pound person is below the usual standard whole-blood donor minimum weight; special eligibility, collection volume, and collection-system requirements govern whether donation is permitted.

book-135-11.questionInPlainEnglish: Which protein is NOT a characteristic concentrated cryoprecipitate constituent?
book-135-11.explanation: Cryoprecipitate contains proteins that precipitate from cold plasma, notably fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII, and fibronectin. Antithrombin is not one of its characteristic enriched components.
optionExplanations: Fibronectin is a recognized cryoprecipitate component.
Factor XIII is retained in cryoprecipitate.
The OCR term refers to von Willebrand-related factor VIII material, which is present.
Antithrombin III is the exception among these characteristic concentrated proteins.
book-135-11.memory: Cryo keeps fibrinogen, VIII, vWF, XIII, and fibronectin.

quickCheck.question: Which abundant clot-forming protein is concentrated in cryoprecipitate?

book-135-11.sourceNote: Factor VIILvW is OCR-corrupted older factor VIII/von Willebrand terminology. Not found means not a characteristic concentrated cryoprecipitate component, rather than proving absolute absence of every trace of antithrombin. The stem's hemophilia treatment framing is historical.

book-135-16.questionInPlainEnglish: What fraction of the starting factor VIII was recovered in the cryoprecipitate?
book-135-16.explanation: Starting activity is 1 IU/mL × 250 mL = 250 IU. Final activity is 9 IU/mL × 10 mL = 90 IU. Recovery is 90/250 × 100 = 36%.
optionExplanations: 11% does not account correctly for both concentration and volume.
25% is below the calculated recovery.
36% correctly compares total final activity with total starting activity.
80% confuses a possible quality threshold with percent recovery.
book-135-16.memory: Yield compares total units, not concentrations alone.

quickCheck.question: How many factor VIII units are in 10 mL at 9 IU/mL?

book-135-16.sourceNote: Shared data verified in PDF page 137: 250 mL at 1 IU/mL becomes 10 mL at 9 IU/mL. The recovered 36% pairing is consistent.

book-135-17.questionInPlainEnglish: Does the cryoprecipitate meet the factor VIII criterion quoted by the book?
book-135-17.explanation: The final bag contains 9 × 10 = 90 IU of factor VIII. That exceeds the book's 80-IU-per-container requirement, so it passes this specific criterion even though recovery is 36%.
optionExplanations: Yes: 90 IU exceeds the cited 80-IU threshold.
The source does not set a minimum percentage recovery for this assessment.
The final amount is 90 IU, which exceeds rather than falls below its threshold.
The shared case supplies concentration and volume, enough to calculate total activity.
book-135-17.memory: A 36% recovery can still leave enough total factor VIII.

quickCheck.question: What quantity decides this book's factor VIII check?

book-135-17.sourceNote: The recovered yes answer agrees with the shared case and source's 80-IU factor VIII criterion. Passing this one criterion does not establish compliance with every current product specification.

book-135-18.questionInPlainEnglish: What percentage of whole-blood platelets reached the platelet-rich plasma?
book-135-18.explanation: Whole blood contains 200,000 × 1,000 × 450 = 9 × 10¹⁰ platelets. PRP contains 300,000 × 1,000 × 250 = 7.5 × 10¹⁰. Recovery is 7.5/9 × 100, about 83%. There are 1,000 microliters in 1 milliliter. Multiply the count per microliter by 1,000 and then by the volume in milliliters to get a total platelet count; the same conversion cancels when comparing the two totals.
optionExplanations: 33% does not match the total-platelet calculation.
45% is lower than the calculated 83%; total PRP platelets must be divided by total starting whole-blood platelets, not inferred from a concentration or volume alone.
66% underestimates the calculated PRP recovery.
83% correctly compares PRP total with whole-blood total.
book-135-18.memory: Count per volume times volume gives the total cargo.

quickCheck.question: Why can't the PRP count alone determine platelet yield?
quickCheck.answer: Yield also depends on component volume.

book-135-18.sourceNote: Shared data verified in PDF page 138: whole blood 450 mL at 200,000/µL; PRP 250 mL at 300,000/µL; concentrate 50 mL at 900,000/µL. Recovered 83% pairing is consistent.

book-135-19.questionInPlainEnglish: What percentage of PRP platelets reached the final concentrate?
book-135-19.explanation: The concentrate has 900,000 × 1,000 × 50 = 4.5 × 10¹⁰ platelets. PRP began with 7.5 × 10¹⁰, so the second-stage recovery is 4.5/7.5 × 100 = 60%.
optionExplanations: 30% is half the correct second-stage recovery.
45% confuses the numeric total of 4.5 with a percentage.
50% would result from comparison with whole blood, not PRP.
60% correctly compares final platelets with their PRP starting pool.
book-135-19.memory: The denominator must match the stage being tested.

quickCheck.question: What is the denominator when calculating recovery from PRP?
quickCheck.answer: The total platelet number in the starting PRP.

book-135-19.sourceNote: The denominator is starting PRP, not starting whole blood. Source data give 60% from PRP and 50% from whole blood; the recovered key is consistent.

book-135-20.questionInPlainEnglish: Does the final platelet concentrate pass the book's stated content requirement?
book-135-20.explanation: The final bag has 4.5 × 10¹⁰ platelets. This is below the cited 5.5 × 10¹⁰ minimum for the specified quality criterion; adequate first-stage recovery does not rescue low final content.
optionExplanations: Yes is incorrect because final content is below the quoted minimum.
The final platelet number is too low, so this is the correct reason.
The book's issue is final content, not the 83% PRP recovery.
The case supplies enough count and volume data to calculate content.
book-135-20.memory: A good first recovery can still finish with too few platelets.

quickCheck.question: What is the final platelet content in this example?

book-135-20.sourceNote: Historical component-QC criterion: the source cites 5.5 × 10¹⁰ platelets per whole-blood-derived concentrate. Current requirements depend on component type and jurisdiction; this does not describe an apheresis-unit target.

book-135-21.questionInPlainEnglish: Which spin should be strengthened to recover more platelets from PRP?
book-135-21.explanation: The first spin separates PRP from red cells. The second spin pellets platelets from PRP; in this exercise, increasing that second spin's time or force can improve recovery into the final concentrate.
optionExplanations: A stronger first spin can trap platelets with red cells and does not address the stated PRP pelleting step.
Increasing the second spin targets the low final recovery and is the keyed adjustment.
Weakening the first spin changes initial separation rather than correcting final PRP recovery.
Weakening the second spin leaves more platelets suspended and can lower recovery.
book-135-21.memory: First make PRP; second collect its platelets.

quickCheck.question: Which spin pellets platelets from platelet-rich plasma?

book-135-21.sourceNote: This is a conceptual historical centrifugation exercise, not a validated operating instruction. Actual platelet production requires the approved process and force-time settings; rpm alone does not specify centrifugal force.

book-135-24.questionInPlainEnglish: For whom is preoperative self-donation NOT advisable in this example?
book-135-24.explanation: Autologous donation means storing one's own blood. Someone already unable to compensate for anemia has too little oxygen-carrying reserve to safely lose more red cells, making that the exception.
optionExplanations: Rare-antigen antibodies can make compatible donor blood hard to find, supporting consideration of self-donation.
Uncompensated anemia makes additional red-cell loss unsafe and is the intended exclusion.
A surgery type alone does not exclude self-donation under the book's approach.
Multiple antibodies can make matched donor units difficult to obtain and may favor considering autologous options.
book-135-24.memory: Self-donation still removes the patient's oxygen carriers.

quickCheck.question: What does autologous donation mean?
quickCheck.answer: Donating blood for one's own later use.

book-135-24.sourceNote: The source reflects older preoperative autologous-donation practice. Present selection and thresholds are individualized under applicable standards; no treatment or donation recommendation follows from this exam key.

book-135-31.questionInPlainEnglish: What expiration does the book assign to refrigerated RBCs after the closed seal is broken?
book-135-31.explanation: Opening the system increases contamination risk. The book shortens refrigerated red-cell storage to 24 hours from opening rather than allowing the original sealed-system expiration.
optionExplanations: Automatic immediate discard is not the book's rule when all other conditions are satisfactory.
The original CPD 21-day shelf life no longer applies after opening.
A 24-hour expiration is the keyed open-system rule.
A six-day closed-system freezing window does not apply to this opened unit.
book-135-31.memory: A broken seal starts a shorter contamination clock.

quickCheck.question: Why does opening a blood system shorten expiry?
quickCheck.answer: It increases the risk of bacterial contamination.

book-135-31.sourceNote: The book's open-system 24-hour rule assumes refrigerated RBC storage and the described break in system integrity. Validated sterile connection systems and specific approved processing can have different implications.

book-135-34.questionInPlainEnglish: Which weak-D donor units are labeled Rh positive?
book-135-34.explanation: A donor unit with detectable D antigen can stimulate anti-D in a D-negative recipient, even if expression is weak. Thus all listed weak-D donor mechanisms are handled as D positive for donor labeling.
optionExplanations: Inherited weak-D expression still means D antigen is present.
A position effect can weaken D expression but does not remove the donor-labeling concern.
Partial D can lack some epitopes while retaining others, so the donor unit is still D positive.
All listed donor weak-D categories are labeled D positive in the book's scheme.
book-135-34.memory: For donors, detectable D means a D-positive unit.

quickCheck.question: Why label a weak-D donor unit D positive?
quickCheck.answer: To avoid exposing a D-negative recipient to D antigen.

book-135-34.sourceNote: Donor labeling is distinct from patient management. Some weak-D genotypes can be managed as D positive as recipients, while others require different interpretation; all weak-D donor categories here remain D-positive-labeled.

book-135-38.questionInPlainEnglish: What identification checks does the book require when receiving externally collected RBC units?
book-135-38.explanation: An independent ABO check helps prevent incompatible transfusion. The source also requires checking the D type of units labeled D negative, where a mistaken negative label could expose a recipient to D antigen.
optionExplanations: ABO on every relevant unit plus D confirmation on D-negative-labeled units is the intended requirement.
Repeating D on all units is broader than the book's stated requirement.
Repeating weak-D testing is not the required confirmation described.
Donor antibody screening is not the identification retest asked here.
book-135-38.memory: Confirm ABO; recheck the negative D claim.

quickCheck.question: Why is an incorrect D-negative label important?
quickCheck.answer: It could lead to D-antigen exposure in a D-negative recipient.

book-135-38.sourceNote: The book's wording means ABO confirmation for all applicable received RBC units plus D confirmation for those labeled D negative. It does not mean ABO confirmation only on D-negative units. Current standards and validated facility policy determine exact checks.

book-135-39.questionInPlainEnglish: What storage temperature does the book assign to liquid RBCs?
book-135-39.explanation: Refrigeration slows red-cell metabolism and limits deterioration while keeping the cells unfrozen. The book's standard liquid-RBC range is 1–6°C.
optionExplanations: 1–6°C is the correct refrigerated liquid-RBC range.
20–24°C is the traditional platelet range, not routine liquid RBC storage.
−18°C is frozen-component storage, not liquid RBC storage.
−65°C is associated with specially prepared frozen RBCs.
book-135-39.memory: Liquid reds rest in the refrigerator.

quickCheck.question: Why refrigerate liquid red cells?
quickCheck.answer: To slow metabolism and preserve viability.

book-135-39.sourceNote: Product-specific textbook storage category; actual storage and expiration follow the component label and current validated standards.

book-135-40.questionInPlainEnglish: What temperature does the book specify for frozen RBCs?
book-135-40.explanation: Glycerol protects red cells during the specified freezing process. The high-glycerol frozen product in this question is stored at −65°C or colder, distinct from ordinary frozen plasma.
optionExplanations: 1–6°C stores unfrozen rather than frozen red cells.
20–24°C is far too warm for frozen storage.
−18°C is not sufficiently cold for the specified frozen-RBC method.
−65°C or colder is the book's frozen-RBC condition.
book-135-40.memory: Frozen reds need colder storage than routine frozen plasma.

quickCheck.question: What protective substance is commonly used when freezing RBCs?

book-135-40.sourceNote: This refers to the high-glycerol frozen-RBC method. Other validated freezing methods can use different temperatures; the recovered −65°C-or-colder key matches the grouped rationale.

book-135-41.questionInPlainEnglish: What temperature does the book assign to fresh-frozen plasma?
book-135-41.explanation: Freezing preserves plasma clotting proteins, including labile factors. The book gives −18°C or colder as the standard frozen-storage category; colder conditions can support different approved shelf lives.
optionExplanations: 1–6°C describes refrigerated thawed plasma rather than FFP kept frozen.
20–24°C is not frozen plasma storage.
−18°C or colder is the book's intended category.
−65°C is sufficiently cold but is a more stringent condition than the standard category asked.
book-135-41.memory: FFP stays frozen to preserve clotting-factor activity.

quickCheck.question: Why is frozen plasma kept frozen?
quickCheck.answer: To preserve its protein and clotting-factor activity.

book-135-41.sourceNote: −65°C also satisfies −18°C or colder, so the literal choices overlap. The key selects the least stringent routine category assigned by the book, not the only temperature that preserves FFP.

book-135-42.questionInPlainEnglish: What temperature does the book assign to unthawed cryoprecipitate?
book-135-42.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is a concentrated cold-precipitable plasma component kept frozen until needed. The book places its routine frozen storage at −18°C or colder.
optionExplanations: 1–6°C does not keep cryoprecipitate frozen.
20–24°C is not its long-term frozen-storage condition.
−18°C or colder is the keyed frozen storage category.
−65°C is colder than required for the standard category, though it satisfies or-colder wording.
book-135-42.memory: Cryo's long storage is frozen storage.

quickCheck.question: Is the frozen cryoprecipitate shelf life applicable after thawing?

book-135-42.sourceNote: −65°C also satisfies −18°C or colder. The intended matching answer is the book's routine −18°C category; the options are not mutually exclusive if read literally.

book-135-43.questionInPlainEnglish: What temperature does the book assign to its conventional platelet concentrate?
book-135-43.explanation: Traditional platelets are stored at 20–24°C with gentle agitation. The warmer environment supports platelet metabolism, while the bag permits gas exchange; this storage also makes bacterial risk important.
optionExplanations: 1–6°C is the conventional RBC range, not the product described.
20–24°C is the textbook conventional platelet range.
−18°C is for certain frozen plasma components, not ordinary platelets.
−65°C is not routine storage for this platelet concentrate.
book-135-43.memory: Conventional platelets stay warm and gently moving.

quickCheck.question: Why is agitation used for conventional platelet storage?
quickCheck.answer: To support gas exchange and maintain the platelet suspension.

book-135-43.sourceNote: Conventional room-temperature platelets are intended. Approved cold-stored platelet products exist under different labeling and indications, so the keyed range is not universal for every modern platelet product.

book-135-44.questionInPlainEnglish: How long does the book allow sealed CPDA-1 red cells to be stored?
book-135-44.explanation: CPDA-1 contains adenine, supporting red-cell ATP regeneration during refrigerated storage. The stated closed-system product has a 35-day shelf life.
optionExplanations: 24 hours corresponds to certain opened-system products, not this intact CPDA-1 unit.
Five days is the book's conventional platelet duration.
35 days is the keyed CPDA-1 shelf life.
One year belongs to specified frozen components, not liquid CPDA-1 RBCs.

quickCheck.question: What energy molecule does adenine help red cells regenerate?

book-135-44.sourceNote: Assumes an intact, properly stored approved CPDA-1 system. Opening, processing, and product-specific requirements can shorten the interval.

book-135-45.questionInPlainEnglish: How long does the book allow FFP to remain stored frozen at its stated routine temperature?
book-135-45.explanation: For its −18°C-or-colder FFP category, the source gives one year from collection. This frozen interval differs from the much shorter expiration after thawing.
optionExplanations: 24 hours is the book's thawed-FFP interval, not frozen FFP shelf life.
Five days is the source's conventional platelet storage interval, not the shelf life of this frozen-plasma product.
35 days belongs to CPDA-1 red cells.
One year is the source's routine frozen-FFP interval.
book-135-45.memory: Frozen FFP: a year in this book; thawed FFP: a different clock.

quickCheck.question: Does thawing preserve the original frozen expiry clock?

book-135-45.sourceNote: One year is the source's routine frozen storage rule. Actual approved expiry depends on temperature and product labeling; it is not the expiry after thawing.

book-135-46.questionInPlainEnglish: How long does the book allow frozen cryoprecipitate to be stored?
book-135-46.explanation: The book assigns one year to frozen cryoprecipitate at −18°C or colder. Once thawed, its much shorter usable interval depends on processing and product rules.
optionExplanations: 24 hours is not the stated frozen-cryoprecipitate interval.
Five days is the conventional platelet interval in this exercise.
35 days is the CPDA-1 red-cell interval.
One year is the keyed frozen-cryoprecipitate shelf life.
book-135-46.memory: Cryo's one-year answer assumes it is still frozen.

quickCheck.question: What major change makes the one-year cryoprecipitate answer inapplicable?

book-135-46.sourceNote: One year refers to the intact frozen product in this textbook. Thawing, pooling, and current product specifications impose different limits.

book-135-47.questionInPlainEnglish: What expiration does the book assign to FFP after thawing?
book-135-47.explanation: The source gives 24 hours when thawed FFP is kept refrigerated. Some products may be relabeled and handled under separate thawed-plasma rules, which are not the same labeled category.
optionExplanations: 24 hours is the book's thawed-FFP limit.
Five days can apply to some separately defined thawed-plasma products, but not this question's keyed FFP category.
35 days is a red-cell preservative interval.
One year applies to the source's frozen rather than thawed plasma.
book-135-47.memory: The label matters: thawed FFP and relabeled thawed plasma differ.

quickCheck.question: At what temperature does the book keep thawed FFP?

book-135-47.sourceNote: The 24-hour answer refers to the labeled thawed FFP category used by the source. Some eligible plasma may be relabeled Thawed Plasma with a longer approved refrigerated interval; do not conflate those categories.

book-135-48.questionInPlainEnglish: What shelf life does the book give platelets in an agitated PL-732 bag?
book-135-48.explanation: The specified gas-permeable bag supports conventional platelet storage at 20–24°C. The source assigns five days; current approved durations also depend on bacterial-risk controls and exact product labeling.
optionExplanations: 24 hours is shorter than the stated intact-system product interval.
Five days is the keyed duration for this bag and method.
35 days belongs to CPDA-1 RBCs and is far too long here.
One year is a frozen-component interval, not conventional platelet storage.
book-135-48.memory: This platelet example pairs a suitable bag with five days.

quickCheck.question: Why can platelet bag material affect storage performance?
quickCheck.answer: Its gas permeability affects platelet metabolism.

book-135-48.sourceNote: Historical named-bag example. Current platelet shelf life depends on the approved bag, product, testing/pathogen-reduction strategy, and jurisdiction; five days is not universal.

book-135-49.questionInPlainEnglish: What refrigerated shelf life does the book assign to CPD blood?
book-135-49.explanation: CPD supplies citrate, phosphate, and dextrose but lacks the added adenine of CPDA-1. In the specified closed storage system, the source gives 21 days.
optionExplanations: 21 days is the correct CPD interval.
35 days belongs to CPDA-1 with adenine.
42 days applies to certain approved additive-solution RBC systems.
CPD is an approved blood-collection anticoagulant-preservative, so this is false.

quickCheck.question: Which extra ingredient distinguishes CPDA-1 from CPD?

book-135-49.sourceNote: The keyed 21-day rule assumes the specified approved closed CPD collection/storage system and correct refrigeration.

book-135-50.questionInPlainEnglish: What refrigerated shelf life does the book assign to CPDA-1 blood?
book-135-50.explanation: Adenine helps maintain ATP and red-cell viability beyond the CPD interval. The specified intact CPDA-1 system therefore has a 35-day shelf life in this exercise.
optionExplanations: 21 days is the shorter CPD interval.
35 days is the keyed CPDA-1 interval.
42 days belongs to certain RBC additive-solution systems.
CPDA-1 is an approved anticoagulant-preservative, not an unapproved one.
book-135-50.memory: Adenine extends this storage example to 35 days.

quickCheck.question: Why does adenine improve red-cell storage survival?

book-135-50.sourceNote: The keyed 35-day rule assumes the specified approved closed CPDA-1 system and correct refrigeration.

book-135-51.questionInPlainEnglish: What shelf life does the book assign to RBCs in AS-1?
book-135-51.explanation: AS-1, also called Adsol, is an additive solution used with prepared red cells. Its nutrients and protective ingredients support the specified refrigerated RBC product for 42 days.
optionExplanations: 21 days is the CPD example, not AS-1 RBCs.
35 days is the CPDA-1 example.
42 days is the keyed AS-1 red-cell shelf life.
AS-1 is an approved additive solution; it is not itself an unapproved storage choice.
book-135-51.memory: AS-1 adds support for 42-day RBC storage.

quickCheck.question: Is AS-1 primarily the collection anticoagulant or a red-cell additive solution?

book-135-51.sourceNote: AS-1 is an additive solution, rather than a collection anticoagulant by itself. The keyed 42 days describes RBCs prepared and stored in an approved AS-1 system.
